vignette:
Peter is a fifty-four-year-old civil servant who works in a municipal permit office, a job that once felt stable and orderly but now feels like a minefield of invisible triggers. He lives with his partner, a woman named Rachel, in a small apartment, and he has been with her for three years—the first relationship he entered after his previous one ended violently. That earlier relationship, with a man named Kevin, had started warmly and then shifted, slowly at first, then sharply. One night, after an argument about Peter staying late at work, Kevin pinned him to the floor of their bedroom, pressed a knee into his chest, and choked him until Peter stopped struggling. The memory of that moment does not come easily when Peter tries to call it up deliberately; he can describe the lead-up and the aftermath, but the core of the event—the seconds when he could not breathe—feels like a gap he cannot reach. Yet the memory returns on its own, unbidden, and when it does it arrives as a series of vivid, still images: the ceiling light fixture, the pattern on the rug, Kevin’s face above him, frozen in a photograph-like tableau. Strangest of all, Peter can taste the event—the metallic tang of his own blood from where his teeth cut his lip, the salt of sweat, and something else, a dusty taste from the carpet fibers that were pressed against his mouth. That taste can surface at any time, triggered by nothing obvious, and when it does he feels a surge of panic.

The triggers that set off these intrusions have grown more specific and more incapacitating over the years. Peter has learned that being alone in a room or a building makes him hypervigilant, waiting for a door to open, so he avoids it at all costs. He schedules his entire day so that he is never without company: he walks into the office with a coworker, eats lunch in the crowded break room, and after work he goes straight to a bar or to Rachel’s side. He has become a constant socialiser, filling every evening with plans—dinner with friends, a trivia night, a walk in a busy park—because he discovered early on that when he is quiet and alone, the images crowd in and the taste floods his mouth, and he cannot bear that. He tells himself that if he keeps moving, keeps talking, keeps his mind occupied, the memories stay at bay. He has also found that he can detach from the memories when they do appear: he learns to watch them as if they are happening to someone else, a mental trick that lets him continue with his day, but the cost is a hollow feeling that grows heavier each week.

At work, the trigger that causes the most trouble is being alone with men. Peter’s boss is a man, and colleagues often ask him to step into a private office to discuss a file. Peter makes excuses—he needs to get coffee, he will follow in a minute, he would rather talk in the open-plan area—knowing that the closed door and the solitary male presence will send his heart racing. He has started to dread weekly one-on-one meetings and has been late on several reports because he cannot bring himself to enter his boss’s office. Another trigger is the sensation of losing control. In his job, this comes up whenever a decision is made for him without his input—a supervisor reassigning a task, a policy change announced without warning—and he feels the same helpless tightening in his chest that he felt on that carpet. Sleeping alone is perhaps the most avoidable trigger: every night he is in bed with Rachel, her warmth and presence a quiet reassurance, but when she travels for work he cannot sleep in their apartment. He checks into a hotel—never alone, he reasons, because there are other guests—but even then he leaves the television on and calls friends until his phone battery dies, terrified of the silence.

The consequences of these habits have accumulated. Rachel has grown frustrated with Peter’s refusal to ever be home alone for an evening; she feels she cannot have a quiet night without him insisting they go out or invite someone over. At work, his avoidance of male colleagues has been noticed; his supervisor mentioned a possible performance review. It was a panic attack in a hotel lobby while Rachel was away—the taste rising, the photographic image of Kevin’s face overlaying the receptionist’s—that finally drove Peter to seek help. He came into therapy because Rachel gave him an ultimatum and because he is exhausted by the constant vigilance. He says he wants to be able to sit still in his own living room without his mind going to that carpet, and he is terrified that the only way forward will mean facing the gap in his memory that he has spent years running from.
